newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian fighting leaves Angkor Wat deserted.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian fighting leaves Angkor Wat deserted.

text.p: Thursday's picture said everything: two Cambodian generals, whose troops fought one another at the weekend, stood smiling together in front of Angkor Wat, world-famous monument to past Khmer glories.
The backdrop, a magnificent 12th century stone temple, was stunning. The smiles were broad.
But the sentiment -- that whatever the differences between Cambodia's warring prime ministers, their two armies are now reconciled -- was false, manufactured for the press and for the moment.

General Mol Reup, military adviser to Cambodia's Second Prime Minister, Hun Sen, whose troops carried out a coup in Phnom Penh over the weekend, insisted on Wednesday that the country is at peace except for a few pockets of Khmer Rouge.
Standing next to him at Angkor Wat, General Tom Sambol, military adviser to deposed First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, shifted from foot to foot as Mol Reup gave his version of reality.

Having elected to remain in Phnom Penh when his faction's troops were driven out over the weekend, Tom Sambol now finds himself in the unenviable position of serving as window dressing for Hun Sen's new government.
It's that or run the risk of being arrested or killed, as has been the fate of some other Ranariddh supporters who stayed behind in the capital.
"I think I will let the government speak for itself," the normally talkative Tom Sambol told reporters on Thursday.
While Phnom Penh and the rest of the country were quiet on Thursday, there is no guarantee that troops loyal to Ranariddh, perhaps in alliance with Khmer Rouge forces, would not counterattack.
Proof that all is not well in Cambodia was everywhere to be seen except in the Hun Sen government's clumsy effort to stage-manage a contrary impression.

The plane that flew the two generals to Siem Reap, near Angkor Wat, left Phnom Penh's Pochentong airport, which was crammed for the third straight day with hundreds of foreign nationals clamouring to be evacuated on mercy flights.
Most were small businessmen and employees of international companies, fleeing what they fear may be the beginning of a protracted period of instability in violence-prone Cambodia.
Angkor Wat, normally overrun with tourists at this time of year, was deserted except for the two generals and a few naked boys swimming in the temple's enormous moat.

A Western reporter who has been living in Siem Reap for the past week said that some townspeople have been dragging bedrolls out to Angkor Wat to sleep at night in the belief that no Khmer faction would dare attack the complex.

And in a sign of the international community's displeasure, the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) decided on Thursday to defer the issue of Cambodia's membership in the group indefinitely.

Observers say the international community, which has invested billions in the Cambodian peace process, may try to use diplomacy to force Hun Sen to reinstall Cambodia's democratically elected government, including Ranariddh.
